clinicalPearls: A benign inherited trait of impaired proximal renal tubular reabsorption of the imino acids proline and hydroxyproline together with glycine
The main gene is SLC36A2 (the PAT2 transporter), with SLC6A20, SLC6A19 and SLC6A18 acting as modifiers of the phenotype
Diagnosed by the characteristic urinary pattern of increased glycine, proline and hydroxyproline with normal plasma levels
Essentially asymptomatic and usually an incidental laboratory finding of no clinical consequence
Newborns physiologically excrete imino acids and glycine until tubular transporters mature at around six months, so the pattern is normal in early infancy
Older weak associations with conditions such as stones or neurological problems reflect ascertainment bias rather than causation
No treatment is needed; the key task is reassurance and avoiding overinvestigation
It should not be confused with hyperglycinaemia or with generalised aminoaciduria of Fanconi syndrome
reference.pathophysiology: Reabsorption of glycine and the imino acids proline and hydroxyproline from the glomerular filtrate depends on a set of proximal tubular transporters, chiefly the proton-coupled amino acid transporter PAT2 encoded by SLC36A2, with contributions from additional transporters that also handle these substrates. When transporter function is reduced, filtered glycine, proline and hydroxyproline are incompletely reabsorbed and appear in excess in the urine while remaining normal in plasma. Because these amino acids are non-essential and the losses are modest, there is no metabolic deficiency or tissue consequence, so the trait is clinically silent.
additionalDifferentials: Physiological neonatal iminoglycinuria before transporter maturation
Isolated hyperglycinuria (a related partial transport defect)
Generalised aminoaciduria of renal Fanconi syndrome
Non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia (a plasma, not urinary transport, disorder)
Secondary aminoaciduria from tubular toxins or heavy metals
Hydroxyprolinaemia and other imino acid metabolic disorders
additionalInvestigations: Urine amino acid chromatography showing raised glycine, proline and hydroxyproline
Plasma amino acids to confirm normal circulating levels
Assessment of other tubular functions to exclude generalised Fanconi syndrome
Family studies, as the trait segregates in relatives
SLC36A2 (and modifier gene) sequencing where confirmation is desired
Repeat testing beyond infancy if the pattern was found in a young neonate
redFlags: Accompanying glycosuria, phosphaturia or proteinuria suggesting generalised tubular dysfunction rather than isolated iminoglycinuria
Raised plasma glycine indicating a systemic disorder such as non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia
Growth failure or acidosis pointing to a tubulopathy
Persistence attributed to disease when the finding is a benign trait
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; iminoglycinuria is a lifelong but harmless trait with no impact on health, growth or life expectancy.
pitfalls: Interpreting the neonatal physiological pattern as a pathological transport defect
Confusing urinary iminoglycinuria with plasma hyperglycinaemia and initiating inappropriate workup
Pursuing extensive investigation or treatment for a benign incidental finding
Overlooking a broader Fanconi syndrome when other solutes are also being lost
references: Broer S et al. Iminoglycinuria and hyperglycinuria are transporter defects
Blau N. Physician's Guide to the Diagnosis, Treatment, and Follow-up of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
